script.title: Why Gold Prices Are Crashing Across India

segments.text: Gold in India just saw its sharpest single-week drop in months.

After racing past record highs near eighty thousand rupees per ten grams, prices suddenly reversed course across Mumbai, Delhi, and Kolkata. That wiped out nearly two thousand to three thousand rupees per tola almost overnight.
For Indian households planning winter weddings, that feels like a festival discount. But inside trading desks and bank vaults, this sudden drop is setting off alarm bells.
Today, we decode why gold prices are plunging, who actually controls the rate you pay at your local jeweller, and why a tumbling gold price can secretly shake Indian lenders.
Here is the weird truth about gold: its price tag in India has very little to do with how much gold Indians are actually buying.

You could see lines outside every Tanishq or Kalyan showroom in your city, and gold prices could still drop like a stone. That is because global gold trades in United States dollars, governed strictly by international bond yields and currency flows.

When global investors expect interest rates in America to stay elevated, international money rushes straight into the dollar. The dollar surges, and gold, which pays zero interest or dividend, suddenly loses its shiny appeal to massive global hedge funds.

Think of it like choosing between lending your cash to a rock-solid borrower paying guaranteed interest, or locking it up in a metal bar inside a locker. When that guaranteed rate looks attractive, funds dump the metal bar to chase yield.

As billions of institutional dollars exit international gold futures, the global price falls. And because India imports over eighty percent of its domestic gold requirement, whatever happens on trading screens in London and New York hits your local bazaar within seconds.
If imports drive the benchmark, why do jewellers in Zaveri Bazaar or Bowbazar still charge you vastly different amounts?

When you buy physical jewellery, you are never just paying for the pure metal. You pay for the gold rate, plus import customs duty, plus three percent GST, and then making charges that range from eight percent to twenty-five percent.

Earlier this year, the Indian government slashed basic customs duty on gold imports from fifteen percent down to six percent. That single policy move aimed to undercut illegal smuggling syndicates and make legal bullion cheaper.

When duty cuts combined with this recent global price correction, the raw price of raw bullion cooled off noticeably. But here is the catch: many retail jewellers immediately padded their making charges, clawing back part of that price drop.
So while ten grams of pure twenty-four carat bullion drops significantly on paper, an ornate necklace for a family wedding often drops by only a fraction of that amount.
Now comes the real danger: what happens when gold prices stay depressed for months?
If you enjoy understanding how money quietly moves across India, hit subscribe right now and join Paisa Decoded.

In India, household gold is not just an emotional heirloom; it is the ultimate credit card for small business owners and families. When an emergency strikes, people do not fill out three-page loan applications; they walk into a Muthoot, Manappuram, or local bank branch and pledge their jewellery.

By regulation, lenders offer up to seventy-five percent of the value of that pledged gold, known as the loan-to-value ratio. If your gold bangles are worth one lakh rupees, the lender safely gives you seventy-five thousand rupees.

Lenders love this loan because if you default, they simply auction your gold to recover their money with almost zero loss. But look at what happens when the underlying market value of gold suddenly tumbles ten or fifteen percent.

Suddenly, that seventy-five thousand rupee loan is sitting against collateral worth barely eighty thousand rupees. If the borrower stops paying monthly interest, the lender's safety cushion completely evaporates.

When that happens, NBFCs are forced to issue margin calls, demanding borrowers deposit extra cash or pledge more jewellery immediately. If struggling borrowers cannot arrange fresh cash, the lender triggers public auctions, flooding the local market with distress-sale gold.
So is gold losing its status as the world's most trusted hedge against financial chaos?
Not even close. While speculative retail traders panic during short-term corrections, the biggest institutional buyers in history are playing a fifty-year game.

The Reserve Bank of India, along with central banks across China, Turkey, and Europe, has been aggressively buying physical gold tonnes for three consecutive years. In fact, RBI recently brought back over a hundred metric tonnes of physical gold stored in London vaults straight back onto Indian soil.

Countries do this not because they expect gold to double by next Diwali, but because gold cannot be frozen by sanctions, cannot be printed by a foreign government, and carries zero counterparty default risk.

For an individual Indian family, gold works the same way: it is an inflation hedge meant to protect purchasing power over twenty years, not a quick-flip intraday trade. Please note, this is strictly educational analysis and not financial advice.

The price fluctuations you see on your phone screen this week are just short-term waves created by currency trades and bond yields. The underlying metal sitting inside Indian vaults and grandmother's almirahs is still the bedrock of the entire country's unwritten balance sheet.

script.description:
Gold prices in India have plunged after touching record highs near ₹80,000 per 10 grams, catching jewellers and wedding shoppers by surprise. In this episode of Paisa Decoded, we break down why international dollar movements and US bond yields trigger sharp corrections in Indian gold markets.

We also dive deep into the hidden mechanics of customs duty cuts, jeweller making charges, and the growing risks inside India's ₹75,000-crore gold loan industry when collateral values drop. Discover why the Reserve Bank of India continues bringing tonnes of physical gold back home despite short-term market crashes.

Subscribe to Paisa Decoded for clear, no-nonsense breakdowns of Indian business, finance, and the economics governing your everyday money.
